units.text: We'll follow a proposed tool call and ask who is allowed to do what. The caller can invoke an approved agent alias. The agent then has its own permissions. If a Lambda action is used, the function separately controls which service may invoke it.

The function's execution role controls the downstream operations it can perform. For a narrow read operation, scope that role to the intended data, and restrict invocation to the authorized agent. Being allowed to invoke a function doesn't give the agent the function's permissions.

In the Agents Classic example, return control gives the application a proposed action and its parameters. It doesn't execute the action. The application checks the current caller, validates the details and obtains any required approval before deciding whether to call the external A P I.

Return only the result associated with the accepted invocation. If policy rejects the action, withhold the tool call and record the rejection. Keep the proposal, actual execution and outcome distinct.
For a high-impact action, show the approver what will change, the intended target and relevant consequences. A general thumbs-up shouldn't authorize a changed parameter or a different resource.
Recheck the authorized action against current state just before execution. If details changed, ask again where required. If approval was denied or expired, stop without making the change.

We'll separate the identity that enters AgentCore from the credential used at a target. Inbound authentication proves who sent the request. The application or configured authorization layer still decides whether that caller is allowed.

For an approved target call, obtain the credential for that target and scope. A user-delegated credential represents a different authority from an application-owned credential. Don't put reusable credentials in a model prompt.

The gateway can check the requested tool and parameters against policy before forwarding. Configure enforcement when the policy needs to stop disallowed requests. Authenticated entry alone does not prove permission for this tool operation.
Log-only mode records what the policy would decide; it doesn't stop the call. Set and verify the intended enforcement mode, and confirm the downstream service also carries out its own access check.

Keep track of the person or service making the request, the agent workload processing it, and the identity used at the target. An A W S service can use scoped A W S credentials; an external service can use its own scoped OAuth credential where supported.

Record the requester and approved action alongside the identity that actually called the target. That preserves the authority chain without recording secret credentials. A shared workload role shouldn't erase user context.

We'll follow one AI workflow from design through ongoing review. Define its intended use and unacceptable outcomes, test representative cases, and make release an explicit decision. Monitor what actually happens in production and use new evidence to revise and retest.
Assign an owner to the release decision, monitoring and remediation. Evidence should show why a version was approved or held. A safety check run once isn't enough when the model, data or use changes.

A meaningful reviewer sees the actual proposal, source evidence, affected resource and impact. Give them a way to reject or ask for more information. A button without sufficient context isn't meaningful oversight.

After approval, check the exact target and current state again before execution. If the decision is rejected or no longer applies, do not execute. Record the reason so the owner can review the outcome.

A Standard workflow can send a request with a task token and wait for a callback. An authorized decision source returns the token and decision. A valid token alone isn't the application's approval check.
Approved, rejected and timed-out paths need different outcomes. Only the approved path can continue to a separately validated action. Reject, expire or safely escalate the others.

Check the approved target and parameters against what exists now. Stop if approval expired or if the request changed materially. A permission to perform yesterday's action isn't authority for a different action now.

If execution partly fails, record what completed before retrying. Use idempotency where supported and run an approved compensation action or escalate when appropriate. A retry must not repeat completed side effects.

We'll verify one agent action using separate evidence streams. The runtime trace shows what the application observed about orchestration. Supported A P I audit records can show calls. The application log records the actual approval and outcome.
Correlate by stable request or action identifiers. Keep only the needed evidence, restrict access and define retention. None of those individual logs tells the full authorization story.

A known single operation can use a direct A P I. A known sequence with auditable transitions can use a deterministic workflow. Consider an agent only when the task genuinely needs interpretation or selection among permitted tools.

A hybrid can let an agent propose an action while the workflow validates it and obtains approval. Regardless of the design, bound retries, costs and authority. The model never becomes the permission decision.
